transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (NovaCore Infra Lead), Maya Singh (NovaCore ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (NovaCore CTO)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
- Ran through kernel selection heuristics and how runtime picks cuBLAS/flash-attention/…
- Discussed observed latency/throughput gaps between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM in our test runs; identified CUDA graph warmup and kernel fusion as likely factors.
- KV cache semantics and prefetching discussed; customer concerned about memory footprint and checkpoint restore time.

[00:00] Alex: okay hello everyone, thanks for taking the time, looks like we have the NovaCore crew, um, and we'll do a deep dive on GPU runtime profiling, basically kernel selection and some direct comparisons, priya is gonna run a couple of benchmarks live and then we'll talk about implications for on-prem/vpc, sound good?
[00:22] Tom: yeah thanks Alex, excited — we want to understand where the extra 15-30% latency is coming from compared to the paper numbers we've seen.
[00:35] Priya: quick note, I'll be referring to TensorRT-LLM (sometimes folks say "Tensort-LLM" in logs) and vLLM (we also see it called "vee LLM") — transcription may garble names, but the configs are in the sheet I shared.
[00:50] Maya: we've run some internal runs on A100s and H100s; for 7B model with batch size 8 latency tail jumps, and throughput isn't matching your published numbers.
[01:10] Priya: okay cool, two high-level places to look: kernel selection & fusion (which influences per-token kernel count) and CUDA graph usage/warmup. Also KV cache behavior changes memory access patterns and can change L2 cache pressure.
[01:34] Liam: can you define kernel selection? we assume the runtime picks optimal kernels automatically, but there are pathologies.
[01:44] Priya: sure — at runtime we have a heuristic that picks between cuBLAS-based matmuls, custom fused attention (flash attention), and vendor-optimized kernels like TensorRT's fused kernels. The choice depends on sequence length, head dims, and where we can fuse softmax + dropout etc. If we pick the wrong kernel per layer you can pay extra memcpy or extra kernel launches.
[02:05] Tom: in our logs we see many small kernels and round-trip overhead, could that be due to kv cache mismanagement?
[02:15] Priya: kinda, yes. KV cache stores past keys/values; if the runtime issues many small kernel calls to append or slice the KV tensors, you'll get launch overheads. Continuous batching and prefix caching can reduce that by reusing a cached prefix and avoiding repeated memcopies.
[02:40] Alex: quick interjection — we'll want to capture actual kernel names from nvprof/nvtx; please share the profiling traces, that helps us map which kernels are dominating.
[02:55] Maya: we have some nvprof traces, though some names are scrambled in our tooling. we'll upload.
[03:05] Priya: perfect. Next point, TensorRT-LLM often wins on throughput because it fuses more operators into fewer kernels and uses CUDA graphs aggressively to amortize launch overhead; vLLM is optimized for batching and scheduling and sometimes does better for low-latency single-stream workloads. The delta depends on the model shape and prompt distribution.
[03:36] Tom: can you elaborate on CUDA graphs? we turned them on but didn't see much improvement.
[03:42] Priya: yeah, common caveat — CUDA graphs are great when the execution graph is static: same sequence lengths and same kernel sequence. But if you have dynamic control flow or variable lengths and you're rebuilding graphs frequently, you pay the graph-construct overhead. Also, graph warmup matters: first few iterations compile/instantiate and then throughput improves.
[04:05] Liam: is there a risk of memory fragmentation with CUDA graphs on long-running on-prem instances?
[04:12] Priya: there can be; if you re-create graphs often without freeing memory properly you can see fragmentation. On Redwood Dedicated we try to reuse graphs across similar workloads, and we also provide heuristics for when to switch to graph mode.
[04:28] Alex: (note) we have a kernel-selection cheat sheet — I'll share post-call with recommended settings per model family.
[04:36] [05:00] -- jump to benchmark notes --
[05:05] Priya: I'm starting a small micro-benchmark now — 7B model, sequence 256, batch 4, on H100, comparing TensorRT-LLM default (with CUDA graphs) vs vLLM baseline with dynamic batching. I'll narrate results as they come.
[05:30] Priya: first run, TensorRT-LLM throughput measured ~210 tokens/sec, p95 latency ~48ms per token with warmup; second run vLLM measured ~170 tokens/sec, but cold-starts on vLLM were better in the 1-stream case.
[05:55] Tom: these match roughly what we saw, order of magnitude difference.
[06:05] Priya: digging into the profiler, I see TensorRT fused kernels named like trt_fused_attn and a smaller kernel count — vLLM has more kernels but sometimes better scheduling for micro-batches. nvtx markers show a lot of small memcpy calls in vLLM path that add up.
[06:34] Maya: we saw memcpys too, mostly when rehydrating the KV cache between requests. Is there a best practice for reducing KV rehydration time?
[06:45] Priya: yes: prefix caching or persistent KV in GPU memory between related requests is the typical approach; for multi-tenant on-prem you may need to trade memory for latency. Another trick is incremental serialization: only transfer delta updates for KV rather than full tensors, but that requires runtime support.
[07:10] Alex: FYI, Redwood's runtime has two KV strategies — ephemeral per-request KV vs. pooled KV that can be reused when prompts share prefixes. We'll share a doc that explains when to enable each.
[07:24] Tom: memory footprint is a concern; at 7B with batch 8 we hit OOM on 80GB nodes with quantization enabled. Thoughts?
[07:36] Priya: quantization helps a lot but interacts with kernels — INT8 or 4-bit quantized matmuls may not have fused attention support in all runtimes, leading to a fallback to higher-precision kernels which increases kernel count. So you can see a paradox: quantization reduces memory but can increase latency if kernel support is incomplete.
[07:58] Liam: so for NovaCore on H100 what's a safe recommendation for 7B?
[08:05] Priya: starts with 4-bit quant and benchmark both with and without kernel fusion. On H100 the best path is typically TensorRT-LLM with CUDA graphs enabled and a small batching window for 7B. We'll run a controlled benchmark to confirm.
[08:22] [08:40] -- discussion of kernel-level artifacts --
[08:40] Priya: profiling shows kernels: cublasGemmEx for matmuls (if not fused), flash_attn_fwd/fused_softmax for attention (when available), and custom trt_fused kernels. Kernel launch overhead from many tiny kernels (tens to hundreds per token) kills latency; CUDA graphs collapse that into a single launch.
[09:02] Tom: how do we know if our codepath is using fused kernels?
[09:08] Priya: look for fused kernel names in nvprof / Nsight; also check timeline for reduced memcpy. Redwood's runtime emits NVTX ranges when we hit fused paths.
[09:18] Maya: we sometimes see an unknown kernel called "_pytorch_..." in traces — is that a JIT fallback?
[09:25] Priya: yes, that's often torchscript/pytorch op wrappers; that indicates the runtime didn't natively replace the op with a vendor kernel. This is a target for optimization.
[09:36] [09:50] -- batching and scheduling tradeoffs --
[09:50] Priya: scheduling matters — vLLM's sharded scheduler batches heterogeneous requests by grouping similar shapes; Redwood's continuous batching does prefix bucketing plus opportunistic micro-batching. For ultra-low latency (<50ms p95) you want small micro-batches and preallocated KV to avoid memcpys. For max throughput you increase batch size, use fused kernels and CUDA graphs.
[10:20] Tom: we have bursty traffic; sometimes 1-2k qps for short windows. Will CUDA graphs help?
[10:30] Priya: they help if the per-request graph is the same; for very bursty heterogeneous requests you might rely more on intelligent batching and less on graphs. A hybrid approach often wins: use graphs for common hot paths and fallback for exotic shapes.
[10:48] Alex: note to capture in notes: include suggestions for autoscale/burst policies on Dedicated.
[11:00] [11:20] -- quantization specifics --
[11:20] Priya: quantization choices: 8-bit dynamic, 4-bit (GPTQ / LLM.int8), and specialized 4-bit kernels. On H100, the vendor INT8 path can be very fast, but accuracy/regression testing is needed. Also watch out for per-token bias drift if quantization is too aggressive.
[11:45] Maya: do you support mixed quantization (first N layers FP16 rest 4-bit)?
[11:51] Priya: yes, hybrid quant schemes are common; Redwood's optimizer suggests layer-wise quant profiles and can roll back if eval metrics drop. We'll share recommended profiles for common models.
[12:05] [12:20] -- VPC / on-prem notes --
[12:20] Tom: for our on-prem we are air-gapped; does Redwood runtime require outbound APIs?
[12:27] Alex: Redwood Private can run in fully offline mode; only the customer control plane connectivity is optional. For KMS you can plug in HSM/KMS locally. We'll share the Private deployment checklist.
[12:40] Priya: note, on-prem has implications for driver versions and CUDA toolkits — mismatched driver/CUDA combos can force fallbacks to less optimized kernels. We recommend testing with the exact stack versions we use in benchmarks (we'll provide a docker image and a manifest).
[12:58] Liam: do you have recommendations for GPU driver/packages for H100?
[13:04] Priya: CUDA 12.x and cuDNN compatible builds we use; also ensure NVIDIA driver 535+ (example) and matching NCCL, and enable MIG if you're slicing GPUs. We'll list exact versions in the doc.
[13:20] [13:40] -- deeper profiling notes --
[13:40] Priya: when you share traces, please include: nvprof/Nsight timeline, the exact model config (heads, hidden size, kv layout), and the command line. We then map hot kernels to potential kernel swapping.
[13:58] Tom: we will upload traces to the secure share. any red flags to look for in the trace?
[14:05] Priya: big signs: many small kernels per token, lots of device-host memcpy, high L2 throughput with low ALU utilization, and frequent graph re-instantiation.
[14:20] Maya: what about memory copies between CPU/GPU for KV? our initial log had something like 30% time in memcpy.
[14:28] Priya: that implies KV is being serialized to CPU between turns; enable GPU-resident KV or persistent session state. For serverless hosted flows that's trickier, but for Dedicated/Private we can keep KV resident.
[14:44] [15:00] -- discussion of observed regressions and mitigations --
[15:00] Priya: another practical mitigation is kernel-reordering at compile/graph capture time: if you can collapse matmul+gelu into a single fused kernel you save a kernel launch and memcopy. TensorRT-LLM does this aggressively; vLLM is more conservative. There's work underway to add more fusions.
[15:24] Tom: latency p95 spikes after model reloads; any cause?
[15:30] Priya: model load will warm caches and instantiate graphs; first few inferences incur JIT/graph build cost. We recommend a warm-up phase after deploy or use snapshot graphs.
[15:45] [16:00] -- live Q&A --
[16:00] Tom: question about licensing — if we use TensorRT-LLM optimizations, any license issue?
[16:06] Alex: TensorRT is NVIDIA licensed; we just configure and ship built kernels per the vendor agreements. We'll include a note about licensing in the follow-up doc.
[16:22] Maya: what about reliability — if CUDA graph fails mid-run do you fallback gracefully?
[16:28] Priya: yes, Redwood runtime detects graph exec failures and falls back to non-graph path; we also track metrics and can auto-disable graphs if error rate climbs.
[16:40] Liam: curious about scheduler fairness across tenants on Dedicated.
[16:45] Alex: we have QoS and capacity isolation options; Dedicated can pin a pool to a customer to avoid noisy neighbor. For multi-tenant Dedicated we use token-level and route-level QoS.
[16:58] [17:15] -- wrapping up benchmarks and artifacts --
[17:15] Priya: summary of takeaway from micro-benchmark: TensorRT-LLM + CUDA graphs wins throughput on 7B H100 for common shapes; vLLM can be better for low-latency single-stream with dynamic batching. KV cache and memcopy behavior were the obvious hotspots for NovaCore's runs.
[17:38] Tom: this is helpful — we'll accept the benchmarking plan.
[17:45] Alex: next steps recap: Priya runs suite, Tom uploads traces, Alex sends kernel cheat sheet and deployment manifest, and we'll reconvene.
[18:00] Maya: also ask — can we get a quick pilot on Dedicated for a 2-week stress run?
[18:08] Alex: yes we'll draft a pilot plan; commercial to follow.
[18:20] [Final minute] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and action items.

Referenced artifacts / links (shared during call):
- Benchmark sheet (internal): https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/tensorrt-vs-vllm
- Kernel selection cheat sheet (will be shared): https://redwood.example.com/docs/kernel-selection-cheatsheet
- NovaCore nvprof traces (uploaded to secure bucket) - link in CRM ticket

End of transcript.
